content: When an HIV test kit or tester produces an error, or when an individual has been recently infected and their immune response has not yet developed, the test results may be inconclusive. Individuals with inconclusive HIV test results should be encouraged to return for retesting after 14 days. Inconclusive results can be confusing and stressful for clients, and they may be challenging for healthcare providers to explain. Post-test counseling is essential to carefully communicate the meaning of an inconclusive HIV status, emphasizing that it does not confirm either a positive or negative diagnosis. Retesting after 14 days is necessary to establish an accurate diagnosis. Since a definitive diagnosis cannot be made on the day of testing, immediate referral to HIV care or initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) is not appropriate. Providers must assist clients in creating a clear follow-up plan and scheduling a retesting appointment. Clients should also be informed about prevention options and the availability and benefits of ART if the retest result is positive. Individuals suspected of having acute HIV infection (AHI) should be closely monitored, as this is a period of high infectiousness due to elevated viral loads. Clients should be educated on how to protect their partners and encouraged to return for retesting in 14 days if their current test result is inconclusive. HIV testing services (HTS) sites, testers, and counselors are responsible for ensuring effective linkage to care. They must provide tailored post-test services that address the specific contexts, settings, and populations they serve. Linkage to care involves establishing a deliberate connection between the patient and the services they require. This is critical for newly diagnosed individuals to initiate treatment and for those re-engaging in care. In some cases, linkage to further testing is necessary, such as after a reactive self-test or for individuals with inconclusive results. For all individuals diagnosed with HIV, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends offering treatment and initiating ART as early as possible, preferably on the same day as diagnosis. People living with HIV who are aware of their status but are not currently on ART should be supported to re-engage in care and start treatment. Retesting can serve as a critical entry point for linking individuals from HTS sites to treatment initiation or resumption. Linkage to prevention services depends on the person’s ongoing needs, risks, and vulnerabilities. While prevention services, such as information on HIV, sexual and reproductive health, and condoms, are beneficial for all individuals testing for HIV, most people testing HIV-negative do not require additional prevention services. However, those at ongoing risk and not currently using prevention interventions may benefit from linkage to specific HIV prevention measures, such as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) or post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for those with recent exposure. Linkage to other services following testing, such as sexual and reproductive health services (e.g., contraception and cervical cancer screening), mental health support, and substance use services, may benefit many clients depending on their needs and circumstances. Some HIV testing services are integrated, allowing clients to receive treatment, prevention, and other services at the same time and location. In other programs, specific linkages must be established to connect clients to relevant services. For example, in settings where dual HIV/syphilis rapid tests are used, programs should prioritize linkage to syphilis treatment and further testing when necessary. WHO emphasizes the importance of rapid ART initiation for all individuals with confirmed HIV diagnoses following clinical assessment. This approach is supported by strong evidence for adults and adolescents and moderate evidence for children. A package of support interventions should be offered to ensure timely linkage to care for all individuals diagnosed with HIV. These interventions include streamlined processes to reduce the time between diagnosis and care engagement, enhanced linkage through case management, support for HIV disclosure, partner services, staff training to provide multiple services, and co-located services. Peer support, including peer counseling and navigation, and quality improvement approaches using data to enhance linkage, are also beneficial. Person-centered care should be the guiding principle for ART initiation, focusing on the health needs, preferences, and expectations of individuals and communities while upholding dignity and respect, particularly for vulnerable populations. People newly diagnosed with HIV should be retested to verify their status before starting ART, using the same testing strategy and algorithm as the initial test. This approach minimizes the risk of misdiagnosis, even in settings where rapid ART initiation is implemented. Clients should be encouraged to start ART as quickly as possible, including same-day initiation when there are no clinical contraindications. Rapid ART initiation is especially critical for individuals with very low CD4 cell counts, as they are at high risk of mortality. However, clients should not be coerced into immediate treatment; they should be supported in making informed decisions about when to start ART. Integrated and co-located services, where HTS and ART are both readily available and ART can be initiated on the same day, facilitate linkage to care and are particularly important for individuals with advanced disease. In health facilities, newly identified individuals living with HIV should ideally begin ART at the same location where they are tested, without needing to navigate multiple rooms or providers. Where co-located services are not feasible, peer support, navigation, and case management can help ensure effective linkage to prevention, treatment, and care. In many countries, the majority of individuals testing for HIV are likely to be HIV-negative due to the declining number of undiagnosed cases. To maximize program impact and cost-effectiveness, it is important to reach HIV-negative individuals at ongoing risk and link them to effective prevention measures, such as PrEP or PEP. HTS should facilitate linkage to prevention services for these individuals. A range of HTS options tailored to clients’ specific needs provides an opportunity to reach high-risk individuals, link them to prevention services, and support their adherence to preventive practices. HTS also plays a role in prevention monitoring, such as regular testing for individuals on PrEP, to identify new infections and initiate ART promptly. Measuring linkage to care is essential for any program providing HTS or HIV self-testing (HIVST). Most programs monitor linkage to care within 30 to 90 days of an HIV-positive diagnosis, track time to ART initiation within 7 to 14 days, and report the number of individuals newly initiated on treatment in the preceding 12 months. However, linkage to HIV prevention following HTS is not routinely monitored but may be reported as part of prevention program data or special projects. Measuring linkage can be particularly challenging for HIVST programs in settings with geographically dispersed facilities. Proxy indicators, such as the number of new ART initiations in a region, may be used. Strategies to measure linkage include monitoring ART initiations at treatment centers, including questions in clinic registers to identify prior HIVST use, conducting population-based surveys, leveraging digital tools, and using mathematical modeling to estimate impact. WHO’s guidelines on person-centered HIV strategic information emphasize the ethical and judicious use of individual health data to monitor the epidemic and guide health system responses. Data collection and monitoring systems should adopt a person-centered approach, focusing on using granular data for impact, building HIV monitoring systems for chronic care, and digitizing health data to enable interconnection across sources.
